headline: Halfway Rock's Big Tide: Pollock Steady, Bass Working the Late Shade
subhead: The full moon is stacking current at the Rock, and the bass have pushed into cooler water while the groundfish hold their ground.
body_markdown:
I was out past Bailey Island Tuesday morning, drifting the ledge off the southern tip while the tide built toward the flood, and I noticed something I always look for this time of year: the herring gulls weren't diving, they were sitting. That tells you the bait's deep, not on top, and sure enough when I dropped a jig it found fish holding tight to the bottom in eighteen feet, right where the current pinches around the rockpile. That's been the story of the bay for the better part of two weeks now — the action is there, but you have to go get it rather than have it come to you.

We're riding a full moon this week, and anyone who's fished Halfway Rock long enough knows what that means: the current there gets serious, and the window to fish it well shrinks down to a tight slack period on either side of the tide change. I've had good luck timing my drifts to hit the last twenty minutes of the ebb and the first half hour of the new flood — that's when the pollock stack up predictably on the northeast corner of the Rock in twenty-five to forty feet, and a three-ounce diamond jig worked with a slow, steady lift will connect. Cod have been scarcer than I'd like to report — a few fish in the eight to twelve pound range came up mixed in with the pollock, but nothing like the numbers we'd see in October. Haddock, if you're hoping, forget it inshore this time of year; that's a fall and winter proposition out here.

Striped bass have given me the most to think about this week, and it comes down to water temperature. South of Cape Cod, the bass have gone nocturnal in the heat, but Casco Bay's Gulf of Maine water stays cool enough that our fish keep feeding through the middle of the day, especially around river mouths and current-swept points. I've been finding them at the mouth of the Presumpscot on the last two hours of the outgoing, working white and olive Deceivers along the current seam where the freshwater meets salt — that temperature break is doing exactly what it should, concentrating bait and pulling bass up onto it. Around Peaks Island, the backside drop-off has been producing schoolie bass to twenty-four inches on soft plastics — five-inch pearl white Slug-Go's on a quarter-ounce jighead, cast up-current and let it swing through the eddy. Nothing enormous, but steady enough that I've put fish in the boat four days out of five.

Cape Small and the outer Harpswell coves have been my most consistent bass water for size. I had a morning last week where three fish over thirty inches came off a ledge just inside Cape Small on topwater poppers at first light — that's the kind of window where the tide, the light, and the bait all line up for maybe ninety minutes before the sun gets too high and the fish slide back down into the depth. Once that happens, switching to a bucktail worked slow along bottom in fifteen to twenty feet has kept the bite going through midday, though the pace slows considerably.

Mackerel are the disappointment of the season so far. The big May runs that light up the whole bay have thinned out, and what's left is scattered and unpredictable — a school here off Jewell Island one day, gone the next. If you find them, small painted diamond jigs or a string of mackerel flies will still produce fast, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. They've become a bonus rather than a target, and that's worth knowing before you burn a morning looking.

Bluefish have shown up in modest numbers mixed with whatever bait schools are moving through the outer bay — nothing like the blitzes you'd hear about further south, but enough that a few boats working near Halfway Rock have picked up cocktail blues in the two to four pound range on small metal lures. It's not a dedicated fishery yet up here, more an incidental catch while you're jigging for pollock, but worth keeping a rod rigged with wire if you're seeing bait get nervous on the surface.

Looking ahead, the moon will start easing off its peak influence by the weekend, which should settle the tides back into a more workable rhythm — less of the aggressive slack-to-full-run swing we've had at the Rock, and more of a gradual build that gives you a longer fishing window rather than a short, sharp one. That's good news for anyone wanting to fish groundfish structure without watching the clock so closely. I'd expect the bass pattern to hold steady as long as we don't get a stretch of unusually warm, still weather that pushes surface temps up and pushes the fish deeper during daylight. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the early flood at Cape Small for bass, then run out to Halfway Rock on the tail of that same tide to work the pollock before the current builds too hard to hold bottom. Bring layers — the fog's been rolling in most mornings, and it doesn't burn off until well past nine most days out here.
